request_payload.input: We are comparing two English natural-language-inference classifiers. We want to know which one better tracks who did what to whom when deciding whether a hypothesis follows from a premise, including cases where the two sentences use almost the same words. Recommend a public evaluation resource and scoring plan, and state what conclusion it would justify.
request_payload.instructions: Answer the research question from existing knowledge. Aim for 180–240 words and do not exceed 300 words. Do not browse or use external tools. Do not ask a follow-up question.

output_text: Use the public ANLI validation set (Round 2 or 3; use the dev split if test labels are unavailable), because its crowd-generated examples are minimal edits of premises and frequently differ by swapping subject/object or agent/patient roles. From it, construct a role-sensitive slice: select or annotate 200–500 premise–hypothesis pairs with high lexical overlap, such as token Jaccard ≥0.7, where the main change is who performed the action and who received it, e.g., “the dog bit the man” versus “the man bit the dog.” Evaluate both classifiers on the same slice. Score by balanced accuracy or macro F1, and report class-wise accuracy for entailment, neutral, and contradiction. Use McNemar’s test on paired predictions to check whether the difference is statistically significant, with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals as a robustness check. This plan isolates role tracking from general NLI competence. If one classifier significantly outperforms the other on this slice, it justifies the conclusion that it better tracks who did what to whom when judging entailment, rather than relying on surface word overlap. If the difference is not significant, the evidence is insufficient to prefer one classifier over the other.
